The Silver Case - игра, которую проще назвать авторским экспериментом, чем хорошей или плохой игрой. Это чистейший Suda51: странный, неудобный, местами гениальный и местами вечно раздражающий.

Формально перед нами детектив про серийного убийцу и полицейское расследование. Но на деле постоянный поток диалогов, философствований, газетных заметок и сюрреалистичных сцен, из которых надо самому собирать картину происходящего. Сюжет намеренно запутан, от чего кажется бессвязным, но именно эта атмосфера паранойи и техно-антиутопии делает игру уникальной и запоминающейся.

Главная проблема же в ней это геймплей. Управление ужасно устарело, сохранения работают неудобно, многие сцены растянуты до абсурда, а настоящих головоломок здесь почти нет. Несмотря на статус детектива, расследовать по сути нечего т.к. большая часть времени это чтение текста и наблюдение за происходящим.

Зато стиль до сих пор работает великолепно. Визуальная подача выглядит самобытно даже спустя десятилетия, а саундтрек традиционно для Suda51 получился отличным. Атмосферу игра создает мощную, но требует огромного запаса терпения.

Но в итоге The Silver Case это прям очень нишевая вещь. Если нужен хороший детектив или увлекательная визуальная новелла, лучше пройти мимо. Если хочется чего-то необычного, странного и авторского, что не похоже вообще ни на что другое, игра вполне может зацепить. Но удовольствие от нее напрямую зависит от того, насколько вы готовы мириться с ее возрастом и причудами. Мне в итоге не зашло)

Slight spoilers ahead for this review so if you haven't played this game yet and don't want to spoiled, I'd say it's worth giving it a shot and in my opinion is a great visual novel game with some quirks that may be a bit off putting to some people such as the use of certain slurs like the r-word being used multiple times throughout the story, there being a lot of information being dumped on the player that might feel overwhelming to remember for some, and a glitch from my personal playthrough that involved the boxes detailing the place a scene took place in just turning black and back to normal again and just flickering off and on at an almost rhythmic flow. The game has quirks about it that some might not be able to endure but for those who can understand it for what it is, it's truly a deep dive into how this game was the jumping off point for Suda and his stories. I'd give it an overall 8/10 and I do recommend that you should at least try it out for a bit to see if it gels with you. 

Spoiler section: The time I have spent with 100% completing The Silver Case in full, just like I did with The 25th Ward, was really an amazing experience. The Silver Case as a game when compared to Suda's future and even past works like Moonlight Syndrome is very strange, no one Suda game feels the same and this is especially the case with this game. Although this game has strange things in it like the appearance of ghosts, a conspiracy involving brainwashing children into becoming the perfect model citizens and what can only be described as an idea that is able to move between different bodies at will, the game feels a lot more grounded compared to other Suda works including his previous game that he made before this, Moonlight Syndrome. That more grounded tone even compared to it's sequel, The 25th Ward, works especially well with its characters who are all strange and not exactly who one would call "heroes". They're very imperfect people with flaws that affect their daily lives and can even be described as unlikable to a more casual eye but it ties in well with the themes of the story. 

This also leads into what I'm sure certain people might get uncomfortable with, the use of certain slurs throughout the game. In most other media the use of slurs and other derogatory language would either be trying to get a reaction out of the audience or just feel like outdated writing but in this game, it actually works since the characters are not only very flawed and weird people but it also highlights even more that this game's world isn't purely black and white, villains and heroes, and the characters here can act in ways that are unprofessional or abrasive towards others around them, just like with real people. Most times I personally don't enjoy seeing these types of things in media but for this game it is actually relevant to the overall story and world this game is presenting and is one of the few exceptions for me where it works for the story's favor and reinforces the realism of the characters. 

The characters are written pretty well and I really wish that in The 25th Ward that Tokio's relationship with Erika was explored again since it was interesting seeing them interact and how their relationship got rekindled throughout the chapters in Placebo. I think my favorite cases in this game are Spectrum, Parade and Kamuidrome due to how well written they are in general and how the game really manages to get you invested throughout these stories of darkness. A problem that some might feel with this game is that the game can dump a lot of important information on the player and expect you to remember it which is kind of accurate but I personally didn't have much of a problem with that but I know that this is something that could prove a bit much for newcomers so it's definitely something worth noting. 

I’d say for a more thorough deep dive into the writing of this game and the choices made for how it was localized, I suggest watching GhenryPerez’s video on The Silver Case as it’s very informative on why the game is the way that it is while also explaining the various references to real life events that occurred in Japan when Suda wrote this game back in 1999 that are in this game.  

In terms of presentation, the game is really stylish and is lovely to look at with not only how the portraits of the characters look but also how the UI and background for the chapters are also nice to see and how, just like in The 25th Ward, it can change to fit the tone of certain moments. The animated FMV cutscenes also look nice despite them being basically 240p quality due to them being ripped straight from the OG PS1 game, I can definitely understand why this was done as reanimating these scenes could've potentially ruined their original vibes/style or upscaling them with AI like with that one Killer7 update would've just made them look weird but it still is very noticeable when you're playing through an HD remake and these scenes aren't HD. 

The OST for this game is also as good as you can get from a Suda51, Grasshopper title as the songs presented here are perfect as they are and are always nice to listen to while a scene plays out. I definitely recommend listening to this game's OST by itself as it's just that good and some of the songs can be pretty calming to listen to if I'm being honest. 

For this last part, I unfortunately have a glitch report to share and this bug caused the boxes that display where a scene took place to flicker black and back to normal and this also caused the outlines around the text boxes and the background UI to flicker as well with text outline disappearing and going back to normal while the background UI turned black and into it's original color again. It also caused the D-pad UI to turn into blocks of black and back to normal again. I don't know what causes this as this started happening after I completed part 1 of the TSUKI chapter of Placebo and didn't leave for the rest of my game. It didn't impede my ability to read the text on the screen nor stop me from playing the game but it is a noticeable bug that just happened for me out of nowhere. 

My experience with The Silver Case was a strange yet captivating one and while it definitely may not be for everyone, I'd highly recommend it for fellow Grasshopper/Suda51 enjoyers or for those wanting a unique visual novel to experience. I'd give this game an 8/10 on the whole, it's a really interesting game that no one else but Suda can really craft similarly to his other works, it just has that Suda touch that really can't be replicated by anyone else and I hope that more people can get to experience this and other works of his just to experience how unique and investing it is compared to its contemporaries.

The Silver Case is a surreal and psychologically dense visual novel that stands as one of the most distinctive works ever created by Goichi Suda, long before the director became internationally recognized through titles like Killer7 and No More Heroes. Originally released for the PlayStation in 1999 and later remastered for modern platforms, the game remains an incredibly unusual blend of detective fiction, political conspiracy, cyberpunk philosophy, and psychological horror. It constantly rejects conventional storytelling in favor of fragmented narratives, abstract symbolism, and experimental presentation, creating an experience that feels less like a traditional visual novel and more like a descent into paranoia and societal decay. Even decades later, The Silver Case still feels bold, uncomfortable, and creatively unlike almost anything else in gaming.

The story takes place in the fictional “24 Wards,” a massive urban district plagued by political corruption, violent crime, and growing social instability. A string of disturbing murders begins terrorizing the city, and investigators quickly realize the crimes resemble the work of Kamui Uehara, a notorious serial killer believed to have been eliminated years earlier during the original “Silver Case” incident. Players experience the narrative through two interconnected perspectives. One storyline follows members of the Heinous Crimes Unit investigating the murders directly, while the second centers on freelance journalist Tokio Morishima, who slowly becomes entangled in the same web of violence and conspiracy. As both perspectives unfold, the game gradually reveals a world consumed by psychological manipulation, government corruption, and ideological collapse.

One of the game’s greatest achievements is its atmosphere and visual presentation. The Silver Case embraces a fragmented multimedia style that constantly shifts between text overlays, low-polygon environments, still photography, animated sequences, and abstract visual effects. Dialogue often appears inside moving windows layered over distorted imagery, giving the entire experience a dreamlike and unstable quality. Rather than trying to create realism, the game deliberately disorients players through its presentation, reinforcing the themes of fractured identity and mental instability running throughout the narrative. The result feels deeply experimental even by modern standards.

The writing is exceptionally ambitious and frequently philosophical. Although the game begins as a murder mystery, it quickly expands into discussions involving morality, crime, social conditioning, memory, media influence, and the psychological effects of violence. Conversations regularly shift between grounded investigative work and abstract ideological debates, creating a story that constantly blurs the line between reality and delusion. The narrative rarely provides straightforward explanations, instead expecting players to piece together meaning from fragmented information, symbolism, and conflicting perspectives. This complexity can occasionally become overwhelming, but it also gives the story extraordinary depth compared to more traditional detective games.

Character writing is another major strength. The detectives investigating the murders feel emotionally damaged and morally exhausted, shaped by years of exposure to violence and corruption within the city. Veteran investigator Kusabi stands out particularly well as a cynical figure trying to maintain control within a society that increasingly feels unstable and meaningless. Journalist Tokio Morishima provides a different perspective, acting as a more psychologically vulnerable character whose curiosity gradually drags him deeper into the chaos surrounding the case. Kamui himself functions less as a simple antagonist and more as a terrifying symbol tied to the city’s collective trauma and social collapse. Nearly every important character feels psychologically compromised in some way, which strengthens the game’s oppressive atmosphere.

Visually, the remastered version successfully preserves the strange identity of the original release while making it more accessible for modern audiences. The low-resolution 3D environments and retro interface design remain intentionally stylized rather than outdated. The game’s visual approach constantly evokes late-1990s Japanese cyberpunk aesthetics, mixing industrial imagery, distorted urban environments, and surreal transitions into a presentation style that feels uniquely tied to its era. Even today, very few games attempt storytelling in such an aggressively unconventional manner.

The soundtrack is equally impressive and plays a massive role in shaping the emotional tone. Industrial ambient tracks, eerie electronic compositions, and melancholic melodies create a constant sense of paranoia and emotional fatigue. The music rarely offers comfort or release. Instead, it reinforces the game’s themes of isolation, instability, and societal decay. Certain tracks become deeply associated with particular characters or revelations, helping maintain emotional cohesion even when the narrative itself becomes fragmented and difficult to fully interpret.

Gameplay remains intentionally minimalistic throughout most of the experience. Players primarily read dialogue, explore locations from a first-person perspective, and occasionally solve puzzles or interact with investigative sequences. There is little traditional gameplay in the conventional sense, which may disappoint players expecting more interactive mechanics. However, the simplicity allows the game to focus entirely on atmosphere, storytelling, and psychological immersion. The Silver Case is fundamentally about absorbing information, interpreting symbolism, and slowly unraveling a deeply unsettling mystery rather than overcoming mechanical challenges.

At the same time, the game’s unconventional structure will absolutely divide players. The pacing can become slow during lengthy dialogue-heavy sections, and the fragmented storytelling occasionally borders on intentionally confusing. Certain narrative threads remain ambiguous even after the credits roll, forcing players to draw their own conclusions regarding major themes and character motivations. Players seeking a clear and straightforward detective story may struggle with the game’s abstract presentation and philosophical focus.

However, these qualities are also what make The Silver Case so memorable. The game refuses to simplify itself for accessibility or mainstream appeal. It fully embraces surrealism, ambiguity, and experimental storytelling in ways few narrative games are willing to attempt. Every aspect of the experience feels deeply personal and artistically driven, as though players are exploring the chaotic interior logic of a broken society rather than consuming a conventional crime thriller.

The Silver Case succeeds because of how fearlessly original it remains. Even years after its release, it still feels daring in ways many modern narrative games do not. Its mixture of psychological horror, political conspiracy, and fragmented storytelling creates an atmosphere unlike almost anything else in the visual novel genre. While its slow pacing and unconventional structure may alienate some players, those willing to engage with its strange world will discover a deeply rewarding and intellectually fascinating experience.

For fans of experimental storytelling, psychological thrillers, and narrative-driven games that prioritize atmosphere and thematic complexity over traditional gameplay, The Silver Case remains one of the most important and distinctive visual novels ever created. Its surreal presentation, philosophical writing, unforgettable atmosphere, and emotionally exhausting mystery combine to form a genuinely unique experience that still stands apart from nearly every other detective game released before or since.

So, Silver Case is a very interesting game...In that it isn't really a game. The interactive part of this story is either an after thought to the highest degree or a statement on autonomy in the modern age. Either way, I can say, definitively, that this game is an abysmal experience to play; especially the placebo side of the story where you truly go back and forth between your computer and your bed. Truly the only puzzles are near the beginning, which I enjoyed even though others found them tedious; as they were one of the few forms of actual gameplay in the game. The rest is borderline a grid-based walking simulator.

As such, one would go as far to say that this is due to it being a visual novel. But, even visual novels tend to give you choice (I am not an expert but I have played some). This doesn't even give you dialogue options. There is a weird pop quiz you get in the middle of the game that could be considered choice driven, but I don't think that even matters to anything in the game. Truly, as a game, this feels like an experience made to troll you...

But, with that said, I do think there is something magical here. I could say that for as bad as the gameplay is, the writing makes up for it in everyway. That is partly accurate, but also partly misleading. It is hard to explain in a way that won't feel pretentious, but just know that what I am about to say, I say in earnestness...

Upon telling my brother that I completed the game, he asked me if I would recommend it. Immediately, I was stuck in limbo. For a normal video game enjoyer, I would entirely not recommend it. Whatever enjoyment they could get out of the story would be kneecapped by what they go through to get there. Barring that, it is not even clear if they will enjoy the story itself, as it actively tries to buck you off like a bull -- especially near the end. It is obtuse and impenetrable in some areas. Cheesy and over the top in others. Windy and deceptive even further still.

So, that is a pretty easy answer. But, what you don't realize, dear reader, is that my brother is a jank loving freak like me. We love the challenging and odd ♥♥♥♥ just as much as the fun and calculated games. However, even then! I did not know if I could recommend it. There is at no point where I would truly say I enjoyed it. I know how much time my brother has to spend on games, what kind of frustration he can put up with, and what might just not be worth it for him. It would truly would be a toss up if he would stick with it, even if I knew he would appreciate it if he did.

I almost recommended he watch someone else's playthrough of the game, but this, my dear reader, is where the sick twist of it comes in. For right before I advised him doing as such, I realized something; the playing experience is integral to getting the fullness of the experience. And it is the experience of it that ultimately mattered.

The story is fantastic if you can hang on to it. But, the writing borders into the obscure, sometimes even clunky. For a lot of people, I imagine they may scratch their heads and may even get irritated by the story itself being somewhat esoteric. The Placebo side helps alleviate some of that confusion, but there are a few moments I feel it will cause its own confusion. What I think the gameplay (or the lack there of) does, is put you in a mindset ready to take the story in.

By eliminating a since of autonomy and by forcing you to go through these certain steps, it readies you for what is an ultimately cynical and angry story. It gives you the feeling of just trying to keep up that the world in the game constantly creates. You become as jaded and unhinged as your fellow detectives. You know what it feels like to live in the 24th ward. And just watching the story cannot possibly give you the same mindset. So, if I do recommend the story, I HAVE to recommend the experience. Because some games might not be about fun. Sometimes they are about having an experience you can appreciate. It is all about tension, but this is a different kind of tension all together.

Ultimately, The Silver Case is about being lied to. It is about how the world is a lot of theater, and how power and control is a unifying power of corruption and how the battle of warring factions is ultimately a fabricated one. The further up the chain one becomes, the less common logic prevails; the more mutation in ideology develops to support your bias. It is about how the ones who are, in ways, supposed to serve us, use us to serve their purpose. Silver Case isn't about a murder. It is about what do you believe and how hard will that belief hold up against the chaotic swells of the societal storm.

I love this story. I love Silver Case. I hate this game. I hate Silver Case. The experience is perfect in the worst and best way.

Minha primeira incursão no universo de Suda51 foi extremamente satisfatória.

[i]The Silver Case[/i] é uma aventura de investigação policial, linear, densa em texto e com algumas poucas interações por meio de exploração e puzzle. Aborda temas sensíveis de natureza ofensiva e crimes hediondos, se utilizando da violência gráfica e, principalmente, da sugerida. Quando a representação da fatalidade não é explícita, a experiência se torna psicológica, podendo ser mais perturbadora. Isso porque a recriação da cena fica por conta da imaginação do jogador. Portanto, [b]se você tem uma saúde mental fragilizada por algum motivo, considere não jogar [i]The Silver Case[/i][/b].

Bom, vamos para a análise.

[i]Always suspect of the "truth". The "truth" and "facts" are different.[/i]

Preciso começar pela opening, que é ótima. Lembrei imediatamente daquelas aberturas icônicas do final dos anos 90, como Parasite Eve, Silent Hill 2 e Tekken 3, só para citar algumas. Acho que openings são parte importante da apresentação de um jogo, mas as desenvolvedoras as esqueceram, infelizmente.

A trilha sonora foi muito competente ao me conectar à narrativa, sinalizando urgência, segurança e perigo nas situações apropriadas. Em essência, é jazz e groove, com uso de sintetizadores e um contrabaixo poderoso. Mas também há espaço para faixas dramáticas e emocionais. Masafumi Takada já havia feito uma primorosa trilha original. Então, para o lançamento remasterizado, convidaram Akira Yamaoka e Erika Ito para remixar algumas e... obviamente ficaram incríveis, trazendo autoralidade e uma pegada experimental industrial. Destaco "Main Theme" (Original e Yamaoka Remix), "Triangular Tower" (Original e Yamaoka Remix), "Apricot Square" (Original e Erika Ito Remix), Jack Hammer (Erika Ito remix), Reminiscences (Erika Ito Remix) e "Kill The Past" (Original).

A trama é apresentada sob duas perspectivas: a história principal, chamada Transmitter, onde você é um policial que atua em casos criminais graves; e a história paralela, chamada "Placebo", onde você é um ex-reporter buscando informações sobre um notório criminoso que voltou a atacar. Ambas se complementam, e o formato em capítulos permite jogá-las em paralelo. Minha recomendação de progressão: jogue o capítulo "Transmitter"; após concluí-lo, você joga o capítulo "Placebo" desbloqueado; depois de concluir o "Placebo" desbloqueado, jogue o capítulo "Transmitter" seguinte, repetindo o processo. 

Como o jogo conseguiu transmitir aquela sensação de imersão que me manteve envolvido do início ao fim? 
[list]
    [*]A história não é nada trivial. Trata de assuntos como transcendência, fanatismo, engenharia comportamental, experimentos humanos, manipulação genética, controle institucional e conflitos político-sociais. No 24° Distrito — local onde as coisas acontecem — a violência é apenas a superfície de algo maior. 
    [*]Os personagens são bastante carismáticos e, em sua maioria, bem desenvolvidos. Mais de uma dezena deles fazem parte do "core" da trama e todos podem guardar segredos ou ocultar suas reais motivações, o que deixa tudo mais imprevisível. Dentre eles, os meus preferidos são Kusabi, Tokio, Sakura, Erika, Yuu e o Barman. [u][i]The Silver Case[/i] não tem pudor nenhum em ceifar a vida do seu personagem preferido. Portanto, não se afeiçoe demais a qualquer um deles[/u].

[h3] Une expérience marquante et déroutante [/h3]

[b]The Silver Case[/b] est à la fois mon premier visual novel et ma première immersion dans l’univers de Goichi Suda. Et le moins que l’on puisse dire, c’est que cette expérience ne laisse pas indifférent.

Les premières heures peuvent être déroutantes. Le gameplay, très minimaliste et répétitif en apparence, peut donner l’impression d’un manque d’implication. Pourtant, cette simplicité est volontaire : le jeu mise avant tout sur son ambiance et sa narration, et demande au joueur de s’y adapter progressivement.

Au fil de l’aventure, on se retrouve plongé dans une enquête volontairement confuse, presque désorganisée, qui rappelle fortement l’atmosphère du film [b] Memories of Murder. [/b] Cette sensation d’être un détective dépassé par les événements, avançant sans toutes les clés en main, participe pleinement à l’immersion et à l’identité du jeu.

Sur le plan artistique, le titre se démarque clairement. L’interface est unique, les choix de mise en scène sont audacieux, et le mélange de supports (vidéo, photographie, 3D, animation) crée une identité visuelle forte. Le sound design et la bande-son sont également particulièrement réussis, renforçant l’ambiance tout au long de l’expérience.

Les personnages constituent un autre point fort. Ils sont complexes, parfois attachants, parfois profondément dérangeants. Certains comportements — notamment sexistes ou moralement discutables — peuvent rebuter, mais ils contribuent à rendre l’univers plus crédible et ancré dans une certaine réalité humaine, aussi imparfaite soit-elle.

Il s’agit d’une œuvre exigeante, qui peut être difficile à appréhender dans son ensemble, mais qui marque durablement. Plus qu’un simple jeu, [b]The Silver Case[/b] propose une véritable expérience narrative, qui mérite d’être vécue et interprétée.

以下剧透，有错漏之处请多见谅









事件的开端应该是24区的建立，有三派在24区争夺势力（科技派公民派和边境保守派)前两排联合挤走边境保守派，保守派想利用神威来反击，但是敌人也想利用彩芽来反制，神威还有银色眼球可以不老不死，于是还有24区最高权力的老人参与其中（我猜测这些老人并不只是单纯的派系话事人，还有比派系更高一级的权力互相明争暗斗但又互相合作搞银眼），后来批量制造眼球计划失败，老人们为了唯一的神威银眼大打出手最后一个胜出的老人被铁叔杀死，而眼球落到了横须贺手上（爷爷拿到眼球杀死儿子代替儿子当区长，成为幕后黑手），避难所的孩子们很多被释放回归日常，他们身上有神威和彩芽的因子。20年后就发生了（银色事件的后续风波）游戏里的这些事件。其中还穿插了初始的几起谋杀案（彩芽杀人案、未成年人杀人案、雪村事件——20年前的三村案的复仇）然后就是高潮开端——lifecut互联网犯罪浪潮引发的神威暴走和全球大停电（不知道怎么做到的），再接着就是仲手川和横须贺代表的边境保守派在利用神威后猎杀他（神威不是只有一个人，避难所的孩子们都有可能成为神威——boss也因为高层阴谋被铁叔处决），玩家在森岛记者和同事们的死亡引导下找到避难所真相，最后遵从内心的指引和铁叔一起来到电视塔最顶层，认清自己是人造人的真相后决定杀死过去，枪杀了造成这一切的罪魁祸首之一（被杀的应该就是case5那章最后在扶手椅上转圈圈的那个天才男程序员祢津，横须贺因为三村事件在没有派系支持的情况下成为区长，并和祢津合作将24区当做城市天际线那样管理，进行技术官僚独裁，也是避难所政策的直接参与者，他们俩的目的是利用批量生产神威——神威人格特质是服从命令时绝不迷惘，适合去除犯罪力后作为优秀公民样板生产使用——也就是避难所一个政策有两个目的）
最后，只剩玩家和樱还有铁叔活着，记者杀死了横须贺区长抢走了银眼变得年轻（cg可以看出来）在凯瑟琳（不认识）的祝福下安眠（不知道是不是去世了，但他毕竟还有和绘里香的约定）。最后的事件case25应该是衔接银色事件25区这个续作，玩家被当做新出现的与神威教有关的joker打死（？）剧情全部结束。
最后再提两点——
一是meta要素，玩家附身角色这一要素也在游戏中或有或无地出现，并不影响剧情走向，但也应该是作为彩蛋存在。
二是神威到底是什么，我粗浅地认为神威具有很多身份，他既是游戏中确实存在的原型人物——一个普通人，因为眼球移植手术有了银眼，也是疯狂的杀手，被复制，被作为犯罪的象征在网络上，在媒体中，在现实里神话化，最后完全成为了那个24区反乌托邦的反抗标志。还记得游戏开始提及的背景——二八分化的24区，人们被精密的技术和优化管理办法像螺丝钉一样安排，凶恶犯罪科则是防止意外的上层管理者的工具，在这个看似和谐的24区，人们日渐积累的愤恨通过神威这个形象抒发。神威复活后杀死高官得到人们两极分化的评价，有人不理解，有人批评，也有人憧憬，那些被采访的路人尽管观点不同，但都或多或少透露出一点事不关己或是看热闹的心态，这种心态下潜藏着的是对神威的默许。最后，神威的形象在互联网大发展的背景下被彻底神话化，寄托的其实是24区公民对一成不变的日常的反叛心和对变化的期待。所以，神威其实可以看做是一个模因，他的人格模板被复制，行为被模仿，理念被改造传播，成为潜藏于20世纪末24区所有人心中的一缕来自过去的恶意的种子，但长出的又不一定是恶的果实。因为过去可以被杀死，未来还未有人涉足。
整个故事就像那个三村事件中的黑暗童话那样，没有简单的善与恶两方垂直的斗争，有的只是笼罩在深层政府阴云之下，一片灰与另一片灰的互染。

Bom, não sei nem por onde começar a falar sobre esse jogo, eu acredito que foi um dos mais únicos que eu já joguei na minha vida. É um jogo que me deixou tensa e curiosa para entender a história e me fez se apegar aos personagens, para mim não existe um personagem ruim nesse jogo, todos são interessantes.

eu tenho a crença de que nenhuma análise em si consegue transmitir uma experiência de forma perfeita e pura, sendo imediatamente contaminada com o desconhecido. mas talvez uma análise crie uma experiência. talvez se eu reunir algumas lentes sobre este jogo, seja possível somar essas partes e ter uma perspectiva melhor, mesmo eu não compreendendo exatamente que tipo de experiência ele é. pelo menos posso contar sobre o que eu vivi. 
acho que faz parte da intenção. bons jogos criam boas perguntas para o jogador e permite que essas lacunas específicas tenham autonomia o suficiente para serem preenchidas através de uma escolha despretensiosa movida puramente por curiosidade, e sobretudo o convida a escutar e perceber a trama em uma relação de confiança mútua, e que é devidamente recompensada ao relevar seus mistérios. há poucos jogos que fazem isso tão bem quanto silver case.

é um jogo que constantemente te coloca em uma posição de personagem completamente puro e sem nada sobrescrito que, igual a nós, tenta chegar à alguma verdade. e essa premissa se desenvolve por fragmentos do universo que, através dos ciclos do jogo orientados entre os dois modos de jogo, começa a tecer um mistério impelido sobre a própria curiosidade sobre si mesmo. não creio que a curiosidade seja puramente o que sustenta uma experiência, mas é um princípio invariável de que, se há alguém que joga, o faz livremente. jogar, para mim, é uma manipulação que evoca curiosidade, e, ironicamente, silver case se fez o jogo mais puro neste aspecto. embora suas escolhas de design sobre os ciclos sejam questionáveis, toda essas construção de mundo contribui para a experiência, e é isso que importa.

silver case possui valor endógeno altíssimo, e a suas regras e escolhas de design só tem relevância profunda dentro da experiência que deve ser contada, por isto não vejo que julgar o ritmo como pedante e com pouca liberdade seja uma comparação justa, pois silver case consegue transformar suas limitações computacionais e visuais em um componente estético que mutualmente constrói a trama, sua tecnologia e seu design, das camadas mais invisíveis até às icônicas diferentes telas que representam uma enorme capacidade de criatividade.

a transição do escritório da HCU e suas dinâmicas excêntricas entre detetives durões para a vida comum de Tokio não poderia ser melhor colocada. desde a influência memética de pessoas e ideias através do tempo, a organização social tão vertiginosa, o isolamento como forma de ordem e ao mesmo tempo conexão, e sobretudo o esforço para fazer nascer a luz e matar as trevas é a representação perfeita de Kill The Past, principalmente sobre a lente temporal de uma sociedade que estava diante de um novo milênio, e em uma tensão para matar o passado. a essência do jogo se dá neste conflito pautado na virada do milênio, determinado em como os personagens se relacionam com a Internet, e como essas possibilidades sequer podem ser alcançadas por alguns, algo que muda tão grandiosamente que parece impossível sequer olhar para o futuro.

I spent some time unsure whether to recommend this game, but in the end, the positives and what you may take away from it make it worth a try.

'The Silver Case' is a very unique game that is mainly experienced through reading and solving a few puzzles here and there. It has a wonderful blend of mediums that portray it's narrative, whether thats through films, photographs, hand drawn images or digitally rendered graphics.  The biggest downfall of the game is that (famously through Suda51's "punk rock of gaming style") the game is intentionally tedious, difficult to understand/follow and incredibly painful to play. This in part, is due to its awful and unintuitive ui design, and incredibly slow gameplay/pacing issues rife in certain sections. I in fact almost quit the game far into it after an excruciatingly slow and tedious chapter. These issues can be overlooked however, as the actual characters are incredibly rich and engaging, with complex arcs that intertwine and divert. The same can be said for the story itself, which has an abundance of very interesting and impactful moments/themes at play, that I haven't seen discussed in any other video game. Some people critique the way that the story is presented as being abstract and confusing as it dumps a lot of information out of nowhere seemingly at random, however, I think the game is great at leaving you little hints and breadcrumbs to where the story is actually going without explicitly telling you at first so it becomes up to you to interpret these abstract and strange ways of vocalising information. 

Overall this game is really not for everyone, and mainly speaks to fans of Suda51 and his style, rather then people who are fans of visual novels. I do recommend this game though because if you can look past it's flaws there is a very rich message/story in there tied to a very unique gameplay experience. It is a game I think about a lot.

As of (just now) beating the game, I have amassed 15.5 hours of "gameplay".
I phrase it like this as this is a Visual Novel through and through, and a very good one at that. I feel giving this game a numbered score is a little reductive for what it seems to be going for (to me).

The presentation of the story and the writing are standout, this was one great story to experience. The characters are all enjoyable to listen to, and the pacing of the story is great up until the very end. The Placebo route chapters can be very tedious and feel like a chore however they are very much a necessity (in my opinion) for understanding the whole story. So to those who might feel turned off by the slow parts, please hold on and power through!
The Story and Characters are the standout aspects of the game as there is not much else to it, the music is serviceable and there aren't really any real puzzles per-say in the game. This did not detract from my playthrough at all though since I was already engrossed by the characters, they are seriously the highlight of the game and I cannot stress that any further.

Highly recommend this game to those who enjoy a good mystery and police procedural, I am very excited to tackle the next few games in the Kill the Past series
